2.6% + 10c with no contract fees, no cancellation fees, no minimum amount of purchases per month. It actually comes out to not be as expensive as most people think.
no chargeback fee is interesting

do you have a specific use case in mind where it's a big advantage? 2.6% + fixed fee seems to me mildly high for a card in the reader + pin entered type of solution. Also chargebacks should be ridiculously rare in this setting.

By contrast, in the European Union there's a cap of 0.3% on credit card interchange rates and 0.2% on debit... there are all-inclusive, Square-like offers for debit card processing fees below 1% for small merchants.
Integrates with all the other Square stuff I assume.
Wow - love the concept and vision here. Were I such a person, I might dub this payments 2.0. This image on their home page gave me chills, though... only because I'm a half-paranoid security geek.
And they say innovation is dead in the U.S. Using the audio jack to read credit cards, brilliant.

The hardware is almost a gimmick to push what is otherwise a potentially powerful service. Individuals are now empowered to take credit cards for anything they previously would have had to take a cash or check for.
You're 100% correct. Hardware is cool, but the merchant services side is what makes Square awesome.

Faster, which is not a trivial thing at all if you've got a line of potential customers... there's additional data on the magstripe that proves the card is really present, which allows you to get better rates with your merchant account.
One commenter said Square has great-looking hardware but pretty mediocre and unattractive software, and that Stripe is doing much better on software.
A customer disliked that during money-tight times the person could see them tap 'other tip' to give $1 instead of the $2 or $5 options, though they said the rest of Square's hardware is on point.
A merchant was frustrated that Square released a $400 all-in-one Terminal just months after they spent $950 on Square's prior setup, which they are still paying off.
A home improvement business owner is wary of electronic payments. On contracts routinely over five figures, Square's ~2.6% fee is a big cut, and adding a surcharge still leaves chargeback exposure.

Nonprofit user complaints: each Square device has different processing fees, and new devices add a fixed $0.10 fee, so there's no incentive to upgrade. Rates run about 1% above a merchant account, more for debit. Many devices don't work with cheap Bluetooth barcode scanners, pushing expensive Socket scanners. No nonprofit discount, while Stripe and PayPal gave half a percent off.
A commenter noted the Square Terminal does not support PIN entry; it relies on chip-and-sign, or on-device verification for high-value Apple and Google Pay payments.
A customer sees Square as a primary offender in spreading tip prompts at places like coffee shops, complaining about being asked to tip before even receiving what they paid for.
Several commenters found the Terminal's lack of a chargeback fee interesting, and one called per-transaction processing overhead 'highway robbery'.
One commenter felt the Terminal's lack of physical buttons is bad for accessibility. They said the boring traditional UK terminals get the job done.
Early reaction to Square's launch: using the phone's audio jack to read credit cards was called brilliant, with the hardware reader seen as overshadowing the service itself.
A commenter was most excited about Square's emailed receipts, hoping to eliminate paper receipts and get near-instant email alerts if their card is used fraudulently.
Commenters noted the original Square swipe reader could not handle chip-and-PIN cards, likely limiting it to the US market.

A business already using Braintree and PayPal subscriptions said Square would be ideal for tradeshows instead of a dedicated sales laptop, but 'the last thing we need is another gateway/merchant company.'
